newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Wary Europeans set to watch Helsinki summit closely.
newsitem.headline: Wary Europeans set to watch Helsinki summit closely.

text.p: A charm offensive by the United States has succeeded in calming European fears that next week's U.S.-Russia summit would cut a deal on NATO's eastwards enlargement over the heads of the allies.

But diplomats say deep suspicions -- particularly on the part of France -- still lurk just below the surface and could burst out into the open unless President Bill Clinton handles his talks with Boris Yeltsin with great caution.

"I do not think there are still any real fears Clinton will go over our heads, the Americans have worked very hard on that. But of course it all depends on what else they offer and how much they push it," said one alliance diplomatic source.

France, long wary of U.S. dominance in the alliance and determined to maintain its independent nuclear stance, has still to signal whether it will abandon plans announced last year to reintegrate into the military wing it abandoned in 1966.

Paris has made such a commitment conditional on a much more visible European component within a revamped alliance capable of taking new post-Cold War missions and to be launched in parallel with enlargement and a new NATO-Russia relationship.

But the two allies have failed to end a squabble over a French demand to share NATO's strategic southern command despite a German effort to sell a compromise involving a five-year delay before any such step.
Clinton and Yeltsin are due to meet in the Finnish capital Helsinki on March 19-20 amid growing expectations they will agree a compromise over NATO's planned expansion into former communist Europe.

The issue, now the number one foreign policy goal of Clinton's second administration, has long soured relations with Moscow despite NATO's offer of a matching deal giving Russia a major role in Europe's emerging 21st century security order.

NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana has been mandated to negotiate the framework for the new partnership and has held three rounds of talks with his Russian interlocutor Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov.

Alliance sources say the two sides have suddenly started making progress and -- though several problems remain to be overcome -- they say it is clear Moscow is now ready for some sort of deal before a special "enlargement summit" next July.
They say Moscow, keen to distance itself from its former satellites, is now pushing for a separate summit, perhaps in May or June, at which its own deal could be endorsed.

Last February, France -- determined the United States should not set the agenda for enlargement on its own -- ruffled several feathers by proposing a big-power summit of Russia, Germany, France, Britain, and the United States.
The proposal, anathema to smaller countries both inside and outside NATO, highlighted European concerns Washington was moving ahead with the policy without sufficient consultation.

Since then, however, the new U.S. Secretary of State Madelaine Albright -- who toured Europe in February -- has gone out of her way soothe European anxieties and sent deputies to brief European capitals on bilateral U.S.-Russia developments.

Deputy Secretary of State Strobe Talbott, Washington's point-man on relations with Russia, has visited Brussels for talks with Solana on several occasions in recent weeks and also held meetings in Paris and Bonn before going to Moscow.

"The big power summit is still lurking away down there somewhere and can be pulled out again if necessary. For the moment, everyone is just waiting to see what Clinton and Yeltsin come up with," added the source.

The United States has recently hinted it does not expect a deal at the summit on more reductions in strategic nuclear weapons -- one area where Europeans could have felt let down -- but says Clinton hopes to make progress on the subject.
Russia has yet to ratify START 11, the Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty, but is keen on extending it to cover sea-based nuclear missiles where there is a huge imbalance in favour of the United States.
